::: {.demo-intro}
**The questions:**
In a shifting digital landscape, how do we identify the risks that matter most to operations?
How do we turn data and findings into actions that make products and digital environments safer?
How do we align business needs with security?

This analysis aims to help guide those decisions using what the data tells us.

:::

## The data

The key word here is **risk**, so it is worth stepping back to look at the concept. Its more
physical sense works well: how **severe** it would be if something happened, and how **likely**
it is to happen at all — keeping in mind that some risks are unacceptable however rarely they
occur.

It is tempting to picture elaborate attack chains, run by a determined, well-resourced adversary,
when most of the time what hits us are attacks of opportunity.

That is why this analysis draws on four sources, each answering something different.

| Source | Answers | Volume |
|---|---|---|
| **NVD** (CVSS) | How bad *would it be* if they exploited me? | ~373k CVEs |
| **EPSS** (FIRST) | How likely am I to be exploited within 30 days? | ~377k CVEs |
| **KEV** (CISA) | What is being exploited *right now*? | ~1.7k CVEs |
| **ATT&CK** (MITRE) | What does the attacker *do* with it? | via CWE → CAPEC |

{{< include _fig/00-setup.qmd >}}

## 1. Severity is not the whole story

Each dot is a CVE, a published vulnerability. The horizontal axis measures how severe it would be;
the vertical one, how likely it is to be exploited.

**The two are related, but far less than you would expect.** Severe CVEs draw attention, since
they promise a bigger reward for the attacker. Even so, we see plenty of exploitation among
vulnerabilities nobody would call critical — more evidence that much of what happens is
opportunistic.

{{< include _fig/01-scatter.qmd >}}

{{< include _fig/02-heatmaps.qmd >}}

{{< include _fig/03-cifras.qmd >}}

::: {.callout-important}
## What severity leaves out

Almost two thirds of what attackers are exploiting **today** scores below CVSS 9.0.

And the other way round: of the tens of thousands of CVEs at CVSS ≥ 9, barely more than **1%** is
being exploited.

Neither figure invalidates severity. What they suggest is that mitigation plans meant to produce
useful action should look at a wider picture than severity alone.
:::

## 2. The strategic cost

The question stops being **how many CVEs to fix**, or **above what severity to fix**, and becomes
how to cover the likely and the severe at once, drawing a clear line at the risks we are not
willing to accept.

If attackers look for opportunity among the easy and the severe, the defence needs the same lens.

{{< include _fig/04-estrategias.qmd >}}

{{< include _fig/04b-simulador.qmd >}}

Read as quadrants, the upper half — the more likely — is where real exploitation concentrates,
and the top-right corner adds the greatest severity to that. Moving the dials shows how much work
each line we draw would cost.

Comparing the two most common policies:

## 3. What the attacker does: MITRE ATT&CK

CVSS and EPSS speak to *how much* and *how likely*. Neither says **what happens next**. For that,
each CVE is chained to the ATT&CK model through its underlying weakness:

```
CVE  →  CWE  →  CAPEC  →  ATT&CK technique
       (NVD)   (MITRE)       (MITRE)
```

{{< include _fig/06-attack.qmd >}}

::: {.callout-warning}
## Beyond the numbers

The difference between intelligence and information lies in interpretation — in applying judgement
case by case.

The CVE → CWE → CAPEC → ATT&CK chain reaches about a third of the vulnerabilities we know to be
exploited, so what follows is a thread to weave into a strategy, not a closed answer.

It is useful for reading *trends* about which offensive capabilities a vulnerability inventory
enables, which can then be checked against technical inventories and the backlog. The limits of
the method are precisely what makes threat intelligence work valuable, once it translates into
concrete action.
:::

Among the vulnerabilities actually being exploited, the most frequent weaknesses are not exotic:
input validation, command injection, out-of-bounds writes, *use-after-free*, unsafe
deserialisation. **They are the same classes of error as two decades ago.** Much of it is caught
by SAST in the pipeline, and prevented earlier still through acceptance criteria in development.
That is where the value of building security into development shows — and the cost of not doing so.

## 4. A worked example: ransomware

So far this describes a method. Let us walk through a case that applies it.

Deciding what is unacceptable — beyond probability — belongs to the business and to whoever keeps
operations running. Say we settle on ransomware as a risk to mitigate at all costs.

The KEV catalog flags which vulnerabilities have confirmed use in ransomware campaigns, so the
path is direct:

{{< include _fig/07-ransomware.qmd >}}

From everything published, we land on a three-figure list. It is not yet a list of actions, since
the specifics of each case call for their own assessment, but it is the raw material a team needs
to build one: cross it against their inventory, see what applies, set deadlines.

Two things worth reading closely.

The first is that **severity does not help you find them**. Median CVSS is the same for the
vulnerabilities used by ransomware as for the rest of the catalog. Were severity the criterion,
more than half of them would stay off the radar. Probability of exploitation, on the other hand,
separates them clearly.

The second is that **many are not new**. About a third were published before 2020, and Microsoft,
Fortinet, Oracle and Ivanti account for a sizeable share. This looks less like chasing
freshly discovered threats and more like a conversation about technical debt and platform
upgrades.

Every organisation is best served by looking at the data and weighing it against its own needs and
resources, to build safer products and digital environments.

## Reproducibility

{{< include _fig/09-repro.qmd >}}

Everything comes from public data and regenerates with a single command
(`python scripts/fetch_data.py`). No client information, private system or real environment was
used.

::: {.nota-ia}
**On the use of AI.** Pulling the four sources, the code that joins them and the charts were built
with AI assistance: that work is mechanical and repeatable, and it is just as well that it is.
The rest is not delegated — what to ask, what to cross-reference, where to move the threshold,
what it means for two medians to be identical, and how far a claim holds without overstating it.
Reading the data, the judgement and the writing are human, limitations included. 
:::
